title: Competing routes back to firing shape population hyperexcitability and its selective suppression
authors: Kamaraj, A. K.; Szuromi, M. P.
abstract: Even within the same neuron, successive spikes can follow distinct trajectories, with afterdepolarization permitting early return to firing and depolarization block prolonging inactivity. Therefore, we propose that hyperexcitability involves changes in the opportunities to fire again from different points across the spike cycle, and not just from quiescence. The hazard of firing - the instantaneous propensity to fire again with time elapsed after a spike - isolates these opportunities. In bursting dopamine neurons, the hazard rises early due to burst-sustaining spikes, falls, then rises again due to burst-initiating spikes. Within a renewal framework, we represent each rise as a competing pathway back to firing and show that recruitment from quiescence and firing again before full recovery provide independent control over population activity. Changes in pathway engagement distinguish subclinical from overt hyperexcitability and allow neurons of the same type to respond differently to a common input. Adding a slower return pathway for drug-bound neurons shows how sodium-channel blockers such as phenytoin and carbamazepine can suppress pathological bursting while leaving physiological activity apparently intact.

title: Super-resolved mass photometry reveals the dissociation pathways of individual protein complexes
authors: O'Shea, A. R.; Bishop, J. L.; Sendker, F. L.; Bardzil, J.; Patel, M.; Peters, J. S.; Hantke, M. F.; Suekawa, M.; Torisu, T.; Uchiyama, S.; Hochberg, G. K. A.; Kukura, P.; Benesch, J. L. P.
abstract: Mass photometry (MP) measures the mass of single unlabelled molecules as they adsorb to a glass surface, but conventional analysis captures each molecule only momentarily, as it binds, and neglects its subsequent fate. Here we correct for coverslip drift and use mass-dependent localisation precision to link successive events at one site to a single molecule and enables two workflows for studying protein assemblies. In tandem MP, matching each binding event with its outcomes yields a two-dimensional precursor-product spectrum that separates dissociation from unbinding, providing structural insights into the protein assemblies and the kinetics of subunit loss. By comparing citrate synthase homologues, we reveal distinct fingerprints and disassembly pathways among complexes of the same oligomeric state. In particle tracking, differential imaging allows for continuous recording of particle mass and position. By examining adeno-associated virus capsids, we recovered accurate masses, and reveals acid-induced disassembly and movement behaviour that depends on both viral and imaging surfaces. Our code is freely available and applies to data obtained on commercial instruments with minimal changes to experimental protocols, offering additional dimensions to MP analysis beyond the mass histogram to return time-resolved, single-molecule histories.

title: Detecting behavioural oscillations with increased sensitivity: A modification of Brookshire's (2022) AR-surrogate method
authors: Harris, A. M.; Beale, H. A.
abstract: A core challenge of cognitive neuroscience is to understand how cognition changes over time within individuals. For example, the tendency for behavioural responses to oscillate over time has been documented extensively in a range of cognitive domains. Recently, however, the phenomenon of behavioural oscillations has been called into question by indications that past findings might reflect aperiodic temporal structure rather than true oscillations. Brookshire (2022) proposed methods to control for aperiodic temporal structure while examining oscillations in behavioural time-courses and found no evidence of behavioural oscillations in reanalyses of four published datasets. However, Brookshire's (2022) method has been criticised for having low sensitivity to detect effects of realistic magnitude, so it is currently unclear whether these findings suggest that behavioural oscillations are not present in these and perhaps many other datasets, or whether they are false negatives. Here, we present a modification of Brookshire's (2022) method that uses an integrated moving average (IMA) model applied to the single-participant data, instead of the original auto-regressive (AR) approach applied to the group-level data. This method demonstrates increased sensitivity to detect effects of realistic magnitude, adequate control of false positives, and other desirable properties such as the ability to increase statistical power by adding more participants. Using this method, we reanalyse the same publicly available datasets and show significant behavioural oscillations in each of them, suggesting oscillations in behaviour are a robust phenomenon upon which to draw theoretical inferences. The participant-level IMA-surrogate method is currently the most sensitive method available for analysing behavioural oscillations while controlling for the contribution of aperiodic data fluctuations.

title: Unexpected Long Range Actions of AAV8
authors: Lahr, J. M.; Ly, J.; Erdem, E.; Williams, M. R.
abstract: Adeno-associated virus vectors (AAVs) have broad utility in neuroscience. A variety of features, such as titer, capsid, enhancers and promoters, coding and non-coding elements, can be utilized to pursue diverse experimental ends. The net effects of titer and capsid have been used experimentally to pursue retrograde and anterograde studies, such as through the monosynaptic spread of high-titer AAV1. The literature on AAV8 is conflicting, with evidence for and against its long-range action outside of the infected starter population. Using the mouse corticopontocerebellar tract, we report that AAV8, when used at high titers, can be associated with long range recombination outside of the starter population. This phenomenon depended upon the viral titer and was influenced by the presence of other experimental injections. Surprisingly, separate injections of high-titer AAV8 recombinase and recombinase-reporter AAV8s gave rise to recombination across long distances in populations not known to be monosynaptically connected. Given the possibility of long range and emergent effects, we suggest that investigators empirically determine titer, capsid, and injection designs that reduce false positives and/or indirect effects.

title: Single-base 5mC and 5hmC profiling identifies a dynamic 5hmC-to-5mC transition at gene bodies and transcription end sites during neuronal differentiation of mouse embryonic stem cells.
authors: Evanich, D. J.; Blum, L. N.; Sen, S.; Campbell, M. A.; Williams, L.; Langhorst, B. W.; Ponnaluri, V. K. C.; Pradhan, S.
abstract: 5-methylcytosine (5mC) and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) are genome-wide epigenetic modifications involved in chromatin organization and transcriptional regulation. Although Enzymatic Methyl-seq (EM-seq) can enable the combined profiling of 5mC and 5hmC, Enzymatic 5hmC-seq (E5hmC-seq) can provide selective profiling of 5hmC at single-base resolution. In this context, we systematically validated E5hmC-seq using diverse genomic DNA samples. Next, we integrated E5hmC-seq with EM-seq to distinguish between 5mC and 5hmC landscapes during neuronal differentiation of mouse embryonic stem cells. First, we observed dynamic remodeling of both modifications throughout differentiation, with pronounced changes during the transition from embryoid bodies (EBs) to neural progenitor cells (NPCs), characterized by a global decrease in 5hmC accompanied by an increase in 5mC. Subsequently, differentially hydroxymethylated regions (DhMRs) exhibiting 5hmC depletion frequently showed a concurrent increase in 5mC, whereas regions gaining 5hmC displayed an opposing trend, reflecting the genome-wide relationship. Mapping these modifications to transcriptional profiles revealed an association between cytosine modification dynamics and gene expression, where transcriptional downregulation correlated with 5hmC depletion with concomitant 5mC enrichment. In summary, combined mapping of EM-seq and E5hmC-seq can decipher the dynamic interplay between 5mC and 5hmC at single-base resolution and provide insights into the relationships among cytosine modification dynamics, genomic context and transcriptional regulation during differentiation.

title: Minimal eukaryotic DNA polymerase zeta/Rev1 GC-pair mutasome
authors: McNellis, C. T.; Brown, M.; Panteleev, D. D.; Zhuk, A. S.; Aksenova, A. Y.; Pavlov, Y. i. I.
abstract: In eukaryotes, translesion DNA synthesis (TLS) enables replication across DNA lesions, difficult DNA structures, and during replicative stress. While TLS prevents replication fork collapse, it is inherently mutagenic and requires tight regulation to prevent global mutation rates increase. Here, we show that elevated DNA polymerase pol {zeta}/Rev1 promotes spontaneous mutagenesis during replication. The five subunits of pol zeta complex (pol zeta5) are the catalytic subunit Rev3, the TLS polymerase Rev1, a dimer of accessory protein Rev7, the Pol31 and Pol32 subunits shared with replicative pol delta. Pol31 and Pol32 bind the Fe-S-containing C-terminal domain (CTD) of Rev3, which serves as a major assembly hub. We found that overproduction of pol zeta5, but not four-subunit pol zeta4 lacking Rev1 or Rev1 alone, increases spontaneous mutation rates by up to 20-fold, indicating that pol zeta5 can access undamaged DNA during replication and compete with replicative DNA polymerases. This mutator effect is independent of PCNA ubiquitylation. augments by hydroxyurea and synergizes with DNA mismatch repair defects. Overproduction of a pol zeta5 complex containing CTD-truncated Rev3 is also mutagenic, demonstrating that active TLS complexes can assemble and function without the canonical CTD interaction hub. Both complexes predominantly generate CG-to-GC transversions, a mutational pattern that resembles several COSMIC cancer mutational signatures. Inactivating Rev3 catalytic activity abolishes mutagenesis, whereas loss of Rev1 catalytic activity substantially reduces mutation rates and eliminates CG-to-GC transversions, identifying Rev1 as the primary cause of the observed mutation pattern. The findings reveal previously unrecognized mechanisms of pol zeta-dependent mutagenesis with broad implications for cellular evolution and cancer development

title: Structural correlates of disease-associated CTSC variants in Papillon-Lefevre syndrome
authors: VONO, F. M.; Naufel, A.; Santos, V.
abstract: Objective: To quantify structural features of disease-associated CTSC missense substitutions and evaluate a structural rule for research prioritization in Papillon-Lefevre syndrome. Design: We compared 16 ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic missense substitutions with 234 recurrent gnomAD substitutions in the mature cathepsin C structure (PDB 1K3B). An expanded exploratory analysis included 35 further literature-indexed substitutions. We audited the documentation used to date the historical holdout and compared AlphaGenome splice scores with a consequence-only baseline. Results: Median predicted destabilization was 2.209 versus 0.763 kcal/mol (AUC 0.764, 95% CI 0.612-0.897). Catalytic proximity was observed in 4/16 versus 9/234. The expanded comparison gave AUC 0.740. Sixteen of 31 substitutions in the historical post-2015 subset had references dated through 2015. For noncoding variants, AlphaGenome splice scores and the consequence-only baseline both obtained AUC 1.000 on 12 positive and 105 negative ClinVar records. Conclusions: Predicted destabilization was associated with ClinVar label status in this dataset. The literature chronology and noncoding consequence composition limit claims of predictive validation.

title: Nuclear quantum effects on ion permeation through the open transient receptor potential melastatin 7 pore: A continuum-electrostatics estimate
abstract: We estimate how nuclear delocalization affects magnesium and calcium release from occupied wells in the naltriben-open pore of transient receptor potential melastatin 7 (TRPM7). We compare the equilibrium distributions of sodium, magnesium, and calcium in the same open structure and fixed continuum field. Thermal quantum states extend over nearby positions, so the ion can sample more than one local environment. For the divalent ions, the model combines a Gaussian test charge in the nonlinear Poisson--Boltzmann potential, spatial dielectric self-energy, and the free-energy cost of restricting a correlated first hydration shell. The hydration shell comprises the water molecules that directly coordinate the ion. In a constriction, the wall can block access to some of these water sites. The classical and quantum calculations use the same insertion energy, pore geometry, and axial diffusivity. The leading Wigner--Kirkwood correction for a smooth ion energy $U_i$ away from the wall is $\ell_i^2\left[\nabla^2 U_i-\frac{\beta}{2}|\nabla U_i|^2\right]$, up to an additive constant, with $\ell_i^2=\frac{\beta\hbar^2}{12m_i}$ for ion mass $m_i$ and inverse thermal energy $\beta$. The length $\ell_i$ is about $0.02\,\text{\AA}$ at $310\,\text{K}$. At the point-ion magnesium basin, the refined centerline self-energy reaches $430\,\text{meV}$. Steric constraints also restrict water coordination at the $1.43\,\text{\AA}$ constriction. At $310\,\text{K}$ in the primary extended dielectric box, the deepest wells for magnesium and calcium lie at $22.75$ and $11.00\,\text{\AA}$, respectively. The quantum changes in mean passage time toward the intracellular and extracellular interfaces are $0.68\%$ and $-0.66\%$ for magnesium and $-0.10\%$ and $16.12\%$ for calcium. Calcium starts on the intracellular side of the constriction and must cross it to reach the extracellular interface. The preferred magnesium site is already on the extracellular side. A change in the dielectric boundary for magnesium or the ligand penalty for calcium can move the deepest well across the constriction and reverse the extracellular response. For comparison, the circular point-ion estimate for magnesium changes from $-37.4\%$ and $-34.5\%$ to $-8.9\%$ and $-8.6\%$ with a $0.5\,\text{\AA}$ wall inset. In the circular reference, the largest local correction occurs at the intracellular widening and depends on near-wall access and axial sampling. Its influence on escape from the occupied well is small. In a separate screened two-ion benchmark, classical repulsion changes escape barriers by tens to hundreds of meV. Isotope substitution tests the mass dependence at fixed charge and chemistry. Together, the results show how pore geometry, dielectric response, and water coordination determine which local quantum corrections affect directional release.

title: Beta-Myosin inhibition in skeletal muscle: Impact of Mavacamten on the diaphragm
authors: Sarfraz, A.; Nayak, A.; Holler, T.; Kraft, T.; Amrute-Nayak, M.
abstract: The diaphragm, a primary respiratory muscle, contains nearly equal proportions of slow, Type-1 and fast, Type-II muscle fibers. Muscle fiber types - classified based on their shortening velocities and force generation abilities - are largely determined by distinct myosin II isoforms. Mavacamten (MAVA), a small molecule inhibitor of beta-cardiac myosin ATPase, is currently used for the treatment of obstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HOCM). Notably, beta-myosin heavy chain (beta-MyHC) is not restricted to the ventricular myocardium but is also expressed in slow fibers, raising concerns about off-target effects of therapy used to treat cardiomyopathic conditions. Given that nearly 50 % of the fibers express beta-MyHC in the diaphragm, we hypothesize that Mava may affect diaphragm muscle activity. Using an in vitro motility assay, we investigated the effects of Mava on native myosins isolated from rabbit diaphragm muscle and measured the velocity of actin and regulated thin filaments. Mava caused a dose-dependent decrease in myosin-driven actin filament velocity, with an apparent IC50 of 1350 nM. Importantly, this inhibition was reversible upon drug washout, indicating a non-permanent modulatory effect. To determine the drugs fiber-type specificity, we tested pure slow- and fast-myosin isoforms from the slow-twitch M. soleus and fast-twitch M. psoas. Both isoforms were inhibited by Mava, but slow myosin exhibited nearly 20-fold greater sensitivity than fast myosin, suggesting a potentially stronger impact on slow fibers. Interestingly, the slow myosin isoform showed even higher sensitivity to Mava than beta-cardiac myosin. Further mechanistic analysis distinguished two modes of action: (i) promotion of the OFF state of myosin, likely reducing a pool of active motors interacting with actin filaments, and (ii) modulation of the actomyosin biochemical cycle. Altogether, given the diaphragms reliance on both fiber types for sustained respiratory function, this off-target effect may impair respiratory performance in patients undergoing therapy, underscoring the need for respiratory function monitoring. The studies have direct implications for understanding the modulation of myosin function under physiological and pathophysiological conditions, as well as following pharmacological interventions.

title: Training background shapes the exercise-induced extracellular vesicle proteome to acute exercise with partial overlap with cold exposure in humans
authors: Tischer, D.; Braunsperger, A.; Schranner, D.; Kallabis, S.; Jost, P. J.; Hasenauer, J.; Meissner, F.; Wackerhage, H.; Soriano-Arroquia, A.
abstract: Aim: Exercise and cold exposure changes circulating extracellular vesicle (EV) and modifies their molecular cargo. However, it remains unclear whether the acute exercise-induced EV proteome response is uniform or shaped by long-term training background, and to what extent it overlaps with the response to cold exposure. We therefore performed an exploratory proteomics study in humans with distinct training phenotypes and compared exercise-induced protein changes with an independent cold exposure dataset. Methods: Serum samples were collected before and immediately after a maximal bicycle ramp test from untrained sedentary controls, endurance-trained athletes, natural bodybuilders, and sprinters. For cold exposure studies, serum samples were collected before, immediately after, and 30 minutes after an ice bath (8-12 degree Celsius) for 5 minutes. EVs were isolated by differential ultracentrifugation and characterized using electron microscopy and nanoparticle tracking analysis. EV proteomics was analyzed by LC-MS/MS. Differential relative protein abundance was assessed within each training group. Shared significance, concordant directionality, functional enrichment, and comparison with the independent cold-water immersion cohort were analysed. Results: Acute exercise altered the serum EV-enriched proteome in all training groups, but the response differed substantially between groups. Sprinters showed the largest number of altered proteins, whereas endurance athletes, bodybuilders, and sedentary controls displayed more selective responses. Few proteins were significantly altered across multiple groups, although a broader set showed concordant directional changes, indicating a limited shared response superimposed on training background-specific remodeling. Functional enrichment highlighted extracellular vesicle and extracellular compartment signatures together with immune, adhesion, trafficking, and stress-response pathways. Cold exposure also induced time-dependent remodeling of the serum EV-enriched proteome, with the largest number of altered proteins observed 30 minutes after exposure. Comparison of the immediate cold response with exercise revealed partial directional overlap, particularly with endurance exercise, but also clear stimulus-specific differences. Conclusion: Our results suggest that changes in the EV proteome profiling after acute exercise are highly dependent on the training background in humans. Rather than revealing a single universal EV protein signature, acute exercise produced group-specific EV proteome remodeling together with a smaller layer of shared directional trends. The comparison with cold exposure supports the concept that acute physiological stressors can remodel concomitant circulating EV protein profiles, while also producing stimulus-specific signatures.

title: Dual mRNA delivery corrects physical and biochemical deficits in a mouse model of hepatic onset trifunctional protein deficiency
authors: von Beck, T.; Terranova, T.; Marayati, B. F.; Zhang, H.; Zhu, L.; Li, S.; Donald, B. R.; Young, S. P.; Lindsay, M.; Todd, C. A.; Koeberl, D. D.
abstract: Mitochondrial trifunctional protein deficiency (TFP-D) is a rare, life threatening long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorder caused by variants in either the HADHA or HADHB subunits, leading to toxic metabolite accumulation and systemic energy deficiency. Current dietary management strategies are only partially effective and fail to prevent long term morbidity and mortality. Here, we developed a lipid nanoparticle (LNP) mediated mRNA replacement strategy to restore TFP function in a moderate severity TFP-D mouse model by delivering both Hadha and Hadhb mRNA. In cultured TFP-D mouse fibroblasts, dual mRNA delivery, but not single subunit replacement, rescued long-chain fatty acid oxidation and revealed a dominant negative effect exerted by the endogenous M404K variant Hadhb. In vivo, intravenous administration of dual mRNA-LNPs restored hepatic TFP expression, reduced circulating long-chain acylcarnitines, and improved physiological performance in aged TFP-D mice. Notably, intravenous delivery of dual mRNA LNPs significantly rescued cold tolerance test (CTT) performance by up to 71.6% compared to untreated and healthy controls. Together, these findings establish dual subunit LNP-mRNA delivery as a promising therapeutic strategy for TFP-D and support its potential applicability to other long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders.

title: MicroBioAgent: an AI agent for automated microbiome analysis
authors: Li, Z.; WANG, J.; Wang, C.; Ding, Y.; Zhang, L.
abstract: Microbiome data analysis demands customized workflows tailored to specific biological questions, sequencing modalities, and data properties. However, constructing and executing these workflows requires navigating heterogeneous software dependencies, reference databases, and multi-step parameter tuning. Here, we present MicroBioAgent, an autonomous, domain-specific agent framework that translates high-level biological queries into executable, study-specific pipelines across 16S rRNA amplicon, reference-based shotgun, and de novo assembly-based metagenomics. Rather than relying on static pipeline templates, MicroBioAgent employs a closed-loop execution architecture: it dynamically selects and runs bioinformatics tools within user-controlled environments while iteratively inspecting intermediate outputs to adapt downstream analytical decisions. Furthermore, to address the long-running nature of metagenomic computation, we introduce an asynchronous background task-management mechanism that reduces LLM token consumption by over 50% while enabling real-time plan adjustment and automated workflow resumption. We systematically evaluated MicroBioAgent across three benchmarks of increasing complexity: (1) paired amplicon and shotgun profiling of tomato rhizosphere microbiomes, (2) taxonomic and functional profiling coupled with machine-learning classification in a colorectal cancer cohort, and (3) de novo metagenomic assembly, metagenome-assembled genome (MAG) binning, and metabolic pathway reconstruction in a polyethylene degradation study. Across all benchmarks, MicroBioAgent faithfully recapitulated the primary biological findings of the original studies, exhibiting high analytical concordance despite expected tool- and database-dependent variations. In systematic robustness evaluations across 27 independent runs spanning three backbone large language models and three prompt-complexity tiers, MicroBioAgent achieved a 98.8% task completion rate and yielded highly reproducible diversity and differential-abundance estimates. MicroBioAgent establishes a scalable, adaptive paradigm for end-to-end computational microbiome research.

title: RADSuite: Improving Species-Level Identification in Microbiome Research
authors: Christensen, R. N.; Gilliland, M.; Young, J.; Manning-Neal, R.; Fan, H.; Lu, S.; Payne, S.; Johnson, W. E.
abstract: In the last twenty years, the microbiome has become a central focus of biomedical research, with amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene considered the industry standard for taxon identification of prokaryotes due to its cost-effectiveness. However, common target regions in 16S amplicons often do not uniquely distinguish closely related species, restricting many analyses to the genus level. Additionally, curated databases such as NCBI's 16S curated database often do not contain all intragenomic variants of the 16S gene and lack annotation of the 16S genomic composition and gene structure. To address these limitations, our team created RADSuite, a collection of tools which includes a more robust database of 16S gene copies (RADlib), an application that identifies which V regions will allow for species level identification (RADx), and a step-by-step guide for how to integrate RADlib within existing metagenomic profiling software tools. Here we demonstrate the utility of using RADSuite as a guide for designing 16S amplicon sequencing experiments. For example, RADx can be used to recommend 16S components that enable species-level resolution for most microbes of interest, even when industry-standard default amplicon choices (V3/V4) are insufficient. These findings suggest that targeted variable region selection is critical for reliable species identification. As researchers use RADSuite to improve the quality of their experiments, we anticipate improved experimental accuracy in fields of microbiome research from human health to environmental conservation.

title: Astrocyte-secreted Cathepsin D regulates hippocampal memory through extracellular matrix remodeling
authors: Kim, H.; Cha, S.; Ji, M.; Kim, G. H.; Shin, S. A.; Lee, S. E.; Lee, K. J.; Lee, S.-W.; Chae, S.; Park, H.
abstract: Astrocytes contribute to hippocampal cognitive functions, but how astrocyte-derived factors regulate memory formation remains unclear. Here, we identify astrocyte-secreted Cathepsin D (CtsD) as a regulator of hippocampal learning and memory. Proteomic profiling of hippocampal astrocytes upon learning identified candidates predicted to be secreted, among which we focused on CtsD, whose extracellular brain functions are unknown. Neutralizing extracellular CtsD or astrocyte-selective CtsD knockdown (aCtsD-KD) impaired hippocampal long term potentiation (LTP) and memory acquisition, suggesting an extracellular role for astrocytic CtsD. In aCtsD-KD mice, these deficits were accompanied by alterations in excitatory transmission and synaptic structures. aCtsD-KD also caused abnormal extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation, and its partial digestion by chondroitinase ABC rescued the memory deficit, indicating that astrocytic CtsD-dependent ECM degradation contributes to hippocampal memory. Together, our findings suggest a CtsD-dependent astrocyte-matrix-synapse axis regulating hippocampal memory.

title: Remarkable Biosynthetic Diversity in the Bionectriaceae: Uncovering the genomic basis of antipathogen bioactivity of cacao fungal endophytes Clonostachys rosea and Waltergamsia zeylanica.
authors: Atencio, L. A.; Castillo, H. E.; Barrios-Jaen, M.; Quintero, I.; Martinez, A.; Rodriguez, C.; Gutierrez, M.; Mejia, L. C.
abstract: Cacao (Theobroma cacao) production in tropical countries is threatened by fungal diseases caused by Moniliophthora roreri and M. perniciosa. Two cacao pod endophytes from Bionectriaceae, Clonostachys rosea TCF417 and Waltergamsia zeylanica TCF400, exhibit growth antagonism towards M. roreri; however, the genetic basis underlying the bioactivity of these strains has not been addressed. Here, we aimed to identify biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) potentially associated with the antifungal bioactivity of these two strains and performed a comparative analysis with 30 publicly available Bionectriaceae genomes using BiG-SCAPE. Whole-genome sequencing using Oxford Nanopore and Illumina technologies, resulted in assemblies of 52.9 Mb (C. rosea TCF417) and 31 Mb (W. zeylanica TCF400). Genome annotation was conducted using Funannotate, and secondary metabolite BGCs were predicted using antiSMASH. The two cacao endophytes harbored 92 BGCs (C. rosea: 67; W. zeylanica: 25), indicating remarkable biosynthetic diversity. Across all 32 genomes, 1,523 BGC-containing regions were identified, most belonging to T1PKS clusters. Network-based clustering revealed 209 gene cluster families (GCFs), of which 52 corresponded to previously characterized BGCs. Conserved BGCs for antifungal compounds, including sorbicillinoids and verticillins, were identified in cacao endophytes and across Bionectriaceae. Additionally, an antifungal assay conducted here demonstrated that verticillin D from C. rosea TCF417 exhibited growth inhibition of plant pathogens Moniliophthora roreri and Mycena citricolor. With about 75% of unassigned GCFs, our results reveal a largely untapped biosynthetic repertoire in the Bionectriaceae and identify verticillin D as a candidate contributor to the antagonism of C. rosea against plant pathogens.

title: EPIC2: integrating single-cell chromatin accessibility with human genetics to identify trait-relevant cell types
abstract: Summary: EPIC2 is a computational and statistical framework for prioritizing trait-relevant cellular contexts by integrating genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics with single-cell chromatin accessibility data. It accounts for linkage disequilibrium when testing for association between GWAS association strength and cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility at both SNP and regulatory-peak resolutions. The resulting P-values are combined using the Cauchy combination test. Availability and Implementation: The core workflow is implemented in R, with source code, vignettes, and reproducible test data freely available at https://github.com/LingxuanZ/EPIC2. Supplementary Information: Supplementary material accompanies this preprint.

title: Syngeneic human iPSC Macrophages and Microglia possess distinct neuroinflammatory profiles, responses to HIV infection, and ART treatment
authors: Oteju, O.; Daniali, M.; Kist, T.; Xu, X.; Emanuel, K.; Niu, M.; Dampier, W.; Fox, H.; Gaskill, P. J.
abstract: Macrophages are innate immune cells that primarily function as professional phagocytes, playing essential roles throughout the body in host defense and maintaining homeostasis. The CNS is populated by two anatomically distinct macrophage populations; parenchymal microglia and border-resident CNS-associated macrophages (CAMs). These populations coordinate the neuroinflammatory response to pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) through Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling and are exposed to distinct microenvironmental cues that could shape their functions. CNS macrophages are also involved in infection with neurotropic viruses such as HIV, where the persistent infection contributes to chronic neuroinflammation and the constellation of other neurological symptoms collectively termed neuroHIV. Although antiretroviral therapy (cART) has transformed HIV care and lessened the severity of many neuroHIV symptoms, the persistence of CNS viral reservoirs and neurological deficits remains a major comorbidity and barrier to cure. Understanding specific contributions of microglia and CAMs to inflammation and neuroHIV has been challenging due to the lack of genetically matched human model systems enabling direct mechanistic comparison between of microglia and CAMs. To address this, we optimized the generation of syngeneic, human-induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derived microglia-like (iMg) and CAM-like (iMacs) cells. These are generated simultaneously from a single donor line and have the same genetic background, enabling side-by-side characterization and functional analyses of inflammation and HIV infection. Transcriptomic profiling by RNA sequencing revealed substantial baseline differences in inflammatory and immune signaling pathways between iMg and iMacs. These intrinsic differences were also observed in TLR-specific NF-{kappa}B responses. Stimulation of TLR4 drove heightened response in iMg relative to iMac, correlating closely with morphological changes, while stimulating TLR2 had a contrasting effect, eliciting a stronger and more robust early NF-{kappa}B response in iMacs. In HIV infection studies, iMacs were more permissive to viral replication at baseline, whereas iMg showed a reduced susceptibility to infection. However, iMacs responded more robustly to cART, while iMg exhibited relative resistance to cART-mediated suppression. These findings delineate fundamental inflammatory and virologic differences between human microglia and CAMs and provide a robust foundation on which to further examine HIV infection, cART efficacy, and immune function in these distinct CNS myeloid populations.
